The fleet of blue sails
The Portuguese man o' war is a colony of organisms that floats on the sea with a sail full of gas.
It lives in the open sea, in warm waters, and lets the wind carry it, just like the by-the-wind sailors and the blue buttons.
Among its tentacles live some little silvery fish, sheltered there: the man-of-war fish.
Moon jellyfish
The moon jellyfish is a transparent jellyfish with no brain and no bones.
It lives near the coast in almost every sea in the world.
The four rings you can see through its bell are its reproductive organs.
The silver shoal
Many small fish swim together in shoals that move as if they were one single body.
They live in the sunlit waters near the surface.
Swimming in a group helps them stay safe: the shoal can open and close again in a moment.
Venus's girdles
Venus's girdle is a comb jelly, a transparent animal shaped like a long ribbon.
It lives in the open sea, in warm and temperate waters, near the surface.
The colours running along its body are not its own light: it is light split by its rows of combs.
Salp chains
Salps are jelly-like animals that can join together in long chains.
They live in the open sea, in every ocean, and swim by pumping water through their bodies.
Although they look like jellyfish, they are closer relatives of vertebrates than of jellyfish.
Sea angels
Sea angels are shell-less sea snails that swim by flapping two fins like wings.
They live in the open sea, mostly in cold waters, alongside sea butterflies.
Sea butterflies are swimming snails too, but they carry a thin, transparent shell.
Fried egg jellyfish
The fried egg jellyfish has a cream-coloured bell with an orange dome in the middle, like a fried egg.
It is very common in the Mediterranean in summer.
Young fish often swim sheltered under its bell.
Iridescent comb jellies
Comb jellies are transparent animals that swim with rows of tiny beating combs.
They live in every sea, from the surface down to great depths.
They are not jellyfish: most of them do not sting, and their combs split light into rainbow colours.
Glass squid
The glass squid is an almost transparent squid.
It lives in the twilight zone, hundreds of metres deep.
The coloured dots on its skin open and close, and that is how it can change colour.
Glass octopus
The glass octopus is an almost transparent octopus: only its eyes and its digestive organ can be seen clearly.
It lives in the open sea, in tropical and subtropical waters, in the twilight zone.
It swims like a jellyfish: it opens and closes the web that joins its arms.
The siphonophore
A siphonophore is a colony of many tiny animals joined together that live as if they were one single organism.
It lives in the open sea and at great depths, where it moves along like a glass train.
Some siphonophores are among the longest animals in the world and can be more than 30 metres long.
The larvacean's palace
The larvacean is a tiny animal like a tadpole that builds itself a house of transparent mucus.
It lives in the open sea; giant larvaceans live hundreds of metres deep.
The house works as a filter to catch its food, and when it gets clogged it makes a new one.
The silk veil
The Deepstaria jellyfish has a very thin, wide bell, like a veil, with a network of channels.
It lives at great depths, hundreds of metres below the surface.
Atolla, the blue siren
Atolla is a dark red deep-sea jellyfish.
It lives in the dark, hundreds of metres deep, in every ocean.
When disturbed, it lights up a wheel of blue light that spins around the edge of its bell.
Vampire squid
The vampire squid is neither a squid nor an octopus: it is the last member of a group of its own.
It lives hundreds of metres deep, in waters with very little oxygen.
When it feels threatened, it turns its cloak inside out over itself and can release a cloud of blue light.
Pyrosomes
Pyrosomes are tube-shaped colonies made of thousands of tiny animals.
They live in the open sea, in warm waters, and rise towards the surface at night.
They make their own light, and when one lights up, the ones next to it answer by lighting up too.
Lanternfish
Lanternfish are small fish with dots of light on their bodies.
By day they live in the twilight zone and at night they rise towards the surface, like hatchetfish.
They are among the most abundant fish in the ocean.
Glass sponge garden
Glass sponges are animals with a skeleton of silica, the same material as glass.
They live on the sea floor, often very deep down.
Inside some of them lives a pair of little shrimps that go in when young and can never get out again.
Sea pens and sea lilies
Sea pens are relatives of corals, and sea lilies are relatives of starfish.
They live attached to the sea floor, and many sea lilies live at great depths.
Many sea pens glow when touched, and feather stars can swim by moving their arms.
Dumbo octopuses
Dumbo octopuses are deep-sea octopuses with two fins on their heads that look like ears.
They live near the bottom, at great depths, in many oceans of the world.
They swim by flapping their fins and opening the web of their arms like a bell.
The river in the mist
The Amazon is the largest rainforest in the world, crossed by the Amazon River and its tributaries.
Scarlet macaws and flocks of parrots fly over the treetops.
The dawn mist forms because the rainforest trees release a lot of water into the air.
The macaws
Macaws are large, brightly coloured parrots with long tails.
They live in the tropical rainforests of the Americas, in the highest part of the trees.
They usually live in pairs, and they often preen each other's feathers.
The toucans
Toucans are birds with a huge, brightly coloured beak.
They live in the treetops of the tropical forests of Central and South America, where they eat mostly fruit.
Even though it is so big, the beak is hollow inside and weighs very little.
Hummingbirds at the heliconias
Hummingbirds are very small birds that can stay still in the air while they drink nectar.
They live in the Americas, and many visit rainforest flowers such as heliconias.
The colour of the throat changes with the angle of the light, because the feathers are iridescent.
The sloth
The three-toed sloth is a mammal that lives hanging from the trees and moves very slowly.
It lives in the rainforests of Central and South America.
Some small moths live in its fur.
Morphos and glasswing butterflies
Morphos are large, bright blue butterflies, and glasswing butterflies have transparent wings.
They live in the tropical rainforests of Central and South America.
The blue of the morpho is not a pigment: it comes from tiny scales that reflect the light.
Emperor tamarins
The emperor tamarin is a small monkey with a very long white moustache.
It lives in the south-west of the Amazon, in Brazil, Peru and Bolivia.
The red-eyed tree frog
The red-eyed tree frog is a green tree frog with red eyes and blue sides.
It lives in the rainforests of Central America and north-western South America.
By day it sleeps stuck to the leaves with its eyes closed, and at night it wakes up.
The dewy spider web
Many spiders weave wheel-shaped webs with threads of silk.
In the damp undergrowth of the rainforest, drops of dew get stuck on them.
Each drop works as a lens and shows the landscape upside down.
Glass frogs
Glass frogs have belly skin so transparent that you can see their organs.
They live in the rainforests of Central and South America, near streams.
When they sleep, they hide their blood in their liver and become even more transparent.
Poison dart frogs
Poison dart frogs are small, very brightly coloured frogs.
The males of some species carry their tadpoles to small pools of water inside plants.
Leafcutter ants
Leafcutter ants cut pieces of leaves to grow a fungus that they use as food.
They live in the rainforests and woodlands of Central and South America.
A small ant often rides on top of the piece of leaf carried by another ant.
Glowing mushrooms
Some mushrooms make their own light, a green light that can be seen at night.
One of these mushrooms grows in Brazil, at the foot of young palm trees.
Its light follows the rhythm of day and night, and attracts insects that can spread its spores.
Fireflies
Fireflies are beetles that make their own light.
They light up at night in damp places, like the rainforest undergrowth.
They use light signals to find a mate.
Capybaras
The capybara is the largest rodent in the world.
It lives near rivers and wetlands in South America, in family groups.
By day, some birds perch on it and pick the parasites off its skin.
Giant water lily
The Victoria amazonica is a giant water lily, with round leaves that can be more than two metres across.
It lives in the calm waters of the Amazon basin.
The flower opens white one night, with beetles shut inside, and the next night it opens pink.
Neon tetras
The neon tetra is a small freshwater fish with a bright blue stripe and a red one.
It lives in the rivers and streams of the Amazon basin.
The blue stripe changes colour with the angle of the light.
The pink river dolphin
The pink river dolphin is a river dolphin with a long snout and a very flexible neck.
It lives in the rivers of the Amazon and Orinoco basins.
When the rivers flood, it goes into the flooded forest and swims among the tree trunks.
The stingrays
River stingrays are freshwater rays that rest on the bottom, often half buried in the sand.
They live in the rivers of South America, including the Amazon basin.
They swim by rippling the edge of their bodies, like a wave.
The arapaima
The arapaima is one of the largest freshwater fish in the world.
It lives in the rivers and lakes of the Amazon basin.
It has to come up to the surface to breathe air, because the oxygen in the water is not enough.
Kilimanjaro at dawn
Kilimanjaro is the highest mountain in Africa, and Kibo is its highest peak.
It rises in Tanzania, near the border with Kenya, above the savanna.
Even though it is near the equator, it has snow and ice on its summit.
The flamingos
The lesser flamingo is the smallest flamingo, pink with coral and black wings.
It lives in shallow salt lakes in East Africa, such as those in Kenya and Tanzania.
It eats with its head upside down in the water, and in groups it puts on displays, moving its head and opening its wings.
The crowned cranes
The grey crowned crane is a tall bird with a crown of golden feathers on its head.
It lives in the wetlands and grasslands of eastern and southern Africa.
It does a dance with bows of the head and leaps with its wings open.
The giraffes at the acacia
The giraffe is the tallest animal in the world.
It lives in the savannas of Africa, where it eats mostly acacia leaves.
It grabs the leaves with a dark tongue about 45 centimetres long, and oxpeckers perch on its neck.
The elephants at the waterhole
The African savanna elephant is the largest land animal in the world.
It lives in the savannas of Africa, in family groups led by an older female.
It sprays water or mud over itself with its trunk, and its ears help it cool down.
The zebras
The plains zebra is a relative of the horse with black and white stripes.
It lives in the savannas of eastern and southern Africa, such as the Serengeti.
Zebras groom each other, standing side by side, head to tail.
The impalas
The impala is a nimble antelope; the males have long, curved horns.
It lives in the savannas and open woodlands of eastern and southern Africa.
It can jump up to 3 metres high.
The warthogs
The warthog is an African wild pig with tusks and warts on its face.
It lives in the savannas of Africa and sleeps in burrows.
It grazes kneeling on its calloused wrists, and when it runs it holds its tail straight up.
The wildebeest river
The wildebeest is a large antelope of the African savanna, with a beard and curved horns.
It lives in the savannas of East Africa, such as the Serengeti.
Every year it migrates in herds of thousands of animals in search of fresh grass.
The hippos
The hippopotamus is a very large mammal that spends the day in the water.
It lives in the rivers and lakes of Africa, and comes out at night to graze.
Its big yawn is a display, and it can walk along the bottom of shallow rivers.
The kingfishers
The pied kingfisher is a black and white kingfisher; next to it is a smaller malachite kingfisher.
They live on the banks of rivers and lakes in Africa.
The pied kingfisher can hover in the air, beating its wings, before diving.
The rhinos and the oxpeckers
The black rhinoceros is an African rhino with two horns, now endangered.
It lives in the savannas and scrublands of eastern and southern Africa.
Oxpeckers pick parasites off its skin and warn it with calls when someone comes near.
Inside the termite mound
A termite mound is the earth nest built by thousands of termites.
In the African savanna, some termite mounds are several metres tall.
In some termite mounds, the warmth of the day moves air through the channels in the wall and the chimney.
The mongooses and the hornbills
The common dwarf mongoose is the smallest mongoose in Africa and lives in families.
It lives in the savannas of East Africa, often inside old termite mounds.
Mongooses and some hornbills look for food together and warn each other when there is danger.
The weavers
The village weaver is a small bird; the male is yellow with a black mask.
It lives in much of Africa and makes colonies of nests hanging from the trees.
The male weaves the nest with long strips of leaf, and the female only adds the lining.
The cheetahs
The cheetah is the fastest land mammal in the world.
It lives in the open savannas of Africa.
The cubs have a mantle of long grey fur on their backs, and their mother calls them with a chirp.
The lions at sunset
The lion is the only cat that lives in groups.
It lives in the savannas of Africa, and there is a small population in India.
Its roar, which can be heard from very far away, announces its territory.
The baobab
The baobab is an African tree with a very thick trunk that stores water.
It grows in the dry savannas of Africa.
Its white flowers open in the evening for one single night, and they are pollinated mostly by bats.
The dung beetles
Dung beetles make balls of dung and roll them along while walking backwards.
They live in the savannas of Africa, and some come out to work at night.
They climb on top of the ball, perhaps to find their way, and some steer by the Milky Way.
The aardvark
The aardvark is an African mammal with long ears, a long snout and strong claws.
It lives in the savannas of Africa, and by day it sleeps in a burrow.
It comes out at night, digs into termite mounds and can move each ear on its own.
The woolly mammoths
The woolly mammoth was a relative of today's elephants, covered in long hair.
It lived on the cold steppes of northern Eurasia and America during the last ice age.
Its small ears and a layer of fat helped it bear the cold.
The smilodons
Smilodon was a large cat with two very long sabre teeth.
It lived in the Americas during the last ice age.
Thousands of its fossils have been found in the La Brea tar pits, in Los Angeles.
The woolly rhinoceros and the giant deer
The woolly rhinoceros had a body covered in hair, and the giant deer had huge antlers.
Both lived on the cold steppes of Eurasia during the last ice age.
The largest known giant deer antlers measure about 3.6 metres from tip to tip.
The megatherium and the glyptodon
Megatherium was a giant ground sloth, and glyptodon a relative of armadillos with a huge shell.
Both lived in South America during the last ice age.
The glyptodon's shell was made of hundreds of bony plates joined together.
The tyrannosaurs
Tyrannosaurus was one of the largest dinosaurs that walked on two legs.
It lived at the end of the Cretaceous, in western North America (Hell Creek Formation).
It probably had lips that covered its teeth, and it made sounds with its mouth closed.
The triceratops
Triceratops was a plant-eating dinosaur with three horns on its face and a large frill.
It probably used its frill to show off to other triceratops.
The ankylosaurus
Ankylosaurus was a plant-eating dinosaur covered in bony plates, with a club at the end of its tail.
It lived at the end of the Cretaceous, in western North America.
The club swung from side to side, mostly from the base of the tail, which was stiff.
The Pyrenean abditosaurus
Abditosaurus was a titanosaur, a giant long-necked plant-eating dinosaur.
It lived about 70 million years ago in what is now the Tremp basin, in Pallars Jussà (Catalonia).
It was about 17.5 metres long and weighed about 14 tonnes.
The velociraptor
Velociraptor was a small dinosaur, the size of a turkey, and it had feathers.
It lived at the end of the Cretaceous in the Gobi Desert, in what is now Mongolia.
Its arm bones keep the marks where large feathers were attached, like those of birds.
The citipati and the nest
Citipati was a bird-like dinosaur with a toothless beak and a tall crest.
It lived at the end of the Cretaceous at Ukhaa Tolgod, in the Gobi Desert, in what is now Mongolia.
Fossils have been found of adults sitting in the middle of their clutch, brooding the eggs with their arms spread out.
The parasaurolophus
Parasaurolophus was a duck-billed plant-eating dinosaur with a long, hollow crest.
It lived at the end of the Cretaceous in what is now Alberta, in Canada.
Its crest, full of passages, could make deep sounds resonate, like a horn.
The pteranodon and the plesiosaur
Pteranodon was a flying reptile, not a dinosaur, and elasmosaurus a plesiosaur with a very long neck.
Both lived at the end of the Cretaceous, in the inland sea that crossed North America.
Pterosaurs probably took off from all fours, pushing off with their arms.
The spinosaurus
Spinosaurus was a very large dinosaur with a tall sail on its back.
It lived in the middle Cretaceous in the great rivers of the Kem Kem, in what is now Morocco.
It was adapted to life in the river, although it is still debated whether it swam or waded.
The yutyrannus and the sinosauropteryx
Yutyrannus was a relative of the tyrannosaurs about 9 metres long, covered in feather-like filaments.
It lived in the Early Cretaceous in what is now Liaoning, in north-eastern China, like sinosauropteryx.
Sinosauropteryx, much smaller, was reddish brown, with a ringed tail and a mask around its eyes.
The iguanodons
Iguanodon was a large plant-eating dinosaur, with a beak and a spike on its thumb.
It lived in the Early Cretaceous; dozens of skeletons were found at Bernissart, in Belgium.
It walked on all fours but could rear up, and it chewed with its cheek teeth.
The archaeopteryx
Archaeopteryx was a small dinosaur with feathers and wings, related to the first birds.
It lived in the Late Jurassic on some islands in what is now Solnhofen, in Germany.
A fossil feather shows that at least part of its plumage was matt black.
The stegosaurus
Stegosaurus was a plant-eating dinosaur with plates on its back and spikes on its tail.
It lived in the Late Jurassic in western North America (Morrison Formation).
Its plates were probably for display, and the spikes on its tail for defence.
The brachiosaurus and the diplodocus
Brachiosaurus and diplodocus were sauropods, huge long-necked plant-eating dinosaurs.
Both lived in the Late Jurassic in western North America (Morrison Formation).
They swallowed leaves without chewing; diplodocus fed closer to the ground.
The ichthyosaurs
Ichthyosaurs were dolphin-shaped marine reptiles, but they were not related to dolphins.
They lived in the Early Jurassic in the sea that covered what is now Holzmaden, in Germany.
They had very big eyes, and a fossil from Holzmaden keeps its smooth skin and a layer of fat.
The eoraptor
Eoraptor was one of the first dinosaurs, small and light, and it walked on two legs.
It lived in the Late Triassic in the Ischigualasto valley, in Argentina.
The layers of volcanic ash in the valley have made it possible to work out the age of the rocks.
The robin in the garden
The robin is a small bird with an orange breast, very common in gardens.
It lives in Europe today, and it is one of the few birds that also sing in autumn and winter.
Like all birds, it is descended from the dinosaurs.
Pegasus
Pegasus is the winged horse of Greek mythology; he was born when Perseus defeated Medusa.
According to the myth, with a kick of his hoof he made a spring gush out on Mount Helicon, the spring of the Muses.
In the scene, Glupòcrates tries out his new wings, flies a loop around the sky and bounces on a cloud as if it were a trampoline.
The griffin
The griffin has the body of a lion and the head and wings of an eagle.
The Greeks told that, far to the north, griffins guarded the gold of the mountains.
In the scene, a sneeze makes the coins jump out of the nest, and a golden bowl lands on its head like a hat.
The phoenix
The phoenix is a fabulous bird that the Greeks linked to Heliopolis, the city of the sun in Egypt.
In the best-known versions, when it grows old it burns in its nest and is reborn from the ashes.
In the scene it falls asleep in its nest, the flames make it disappear and out of the ashes comes a chick with a moustache.
The dragon of the golden apples
Ladon was the dragon that guarded the tree of the golden apples in the garden of the Hesperides, at the western end of the world.
Getting those apples was one of the twelve labours of Heracles.
In the scene, instead of guarding them, he eats them until he is as round as a ball and cannot fly.
Cerberus
Cerberus is the three-headed dog that guards the gate of the world of the dead.
Orpheus, the great musician, charmed him with his lyre so that he could go in to look for Eurydice.
In the scene, the three heads fall asleep to the music, and the smallest one opens an eye and winks at Orpheus.
The hydra
The Lernaean hydra was a many-headed water serpent that lived in a marsh.
According to the myth, when one head was cut off two grew back; Heracles defeated it.
In the scene, every sneeze makes two new heads grow, and all five end up singing like a choir.
The chimera
The chimera was a monster from Lycia with the body of a lion, a goat's head on its back and a snake for a tail.
It breathed fire, and it was defeated by the hero Bellerophon, riding on Pegasus.
In the scene, the lion toasts bread with its fiery breath, but the goat and the snake eat it.
The minotaur
The minotaur, half man and half bull, lived shut away in the labyrinth of Knossos, in Crete.
Theseus found him and found his way out of the labyrinth thanks to the thread Ariadne had given him.
In the scene, lost in his own labyrinth, he follows a red thread until he is wrapped up like a parcel.
The centaur
Centaurs were half man and half horse, and they lived on Mount Pelion, in Thessaly.
The wisest was Chiron, who played the lyre and was the teacher of heroes such as Achilles.
In the scene, he dances with his lyre, gets his four legs tangled and ends up sitting down playing.
Medusa
Medusa was a gorgon with snakes for hair, and whoever looked at her turned to stone.
Perseus defeated her without looking at her directly, seeing her reflected in his bronze shield.
In the scene, Glupòcrates admires himself in the mirror of the shield and turns himself to stone.
The siren
The Greek sirens were half woman and half bird, and with their song they made sailors shipwreck.
Odysseus had himself tied to the ship's mast to hear them, and his sailors blocked their ears with wax.
In the scene, the siren's highest note is so out of tune that the ship rows away.
The pinya
The pinya is the base of the castell: many people hugging together who hold it up and would cushion a fall.
The taller the castell, the more people are needed in the pinya.
In 2010, UNESCO declared castells Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
The baixos and the segons
The baixos are the first level of the trunk and bear the weight of the whole castell.
The segons climb up their backs until they stand on the shoulders of the baixos.
Castellers climb barefoot, so as not to hurt their companions and to feel better where they step.
The terços and the quarts
The trunk is the part of the castell where every level has the same number of people.
In a seven-level castell, the trunk has baixos, segons, terços and quarts.
The tightly wrapped sash protects the back and works as a handhold for climbing.
The dosos
The pom de dalt is the top of the castell, made by children who weigh little.
The dosos are the two castellers who hold on to each other under the acotxador and the enxaneta.
Like the whole pom de dalt, they wear helmets for protection.
The acotxador
The acotxador crouches on top of the dosos and works as a step so that the enxaneta can climb.
The name comes from «acotxar-se», which means to crouch down in Catalan.
The enxaneta and the aleta
The enxaneta is the smallest casteller and the one who crowns the castell.
When they reach the very top they raise a hand: that is the aleta, the gesture that says the castell has been loaded.
The castell of three
In a castell of three, each level of the trunk has three people.
The name gives the people per level and the levels: a three of seven has three people per level and seven levels.
It is one of the castells most often seen in the squares.
The tower
The tower, or castell of two, has two people on each level.
It is narrower than a castell of three and harder to keep balanced.
The castell of four
In a castell of four, each level of the trunk has four people.
A four of seven has four people per level and seven levels.
Unloading the castell
The castell does not end with the aleta: afterwards it has to be taken down level by level, from top to bottom.
If it reaches the aleta it is said to be loaded, and if it is also taken down without falling, it is unloaded.
In the activity, the castell comes down little by little and never falls.
The town festival
Castells are built in the square, often during the town festival, in front of the town hall or the church.
Each colla (team) has its own shirt colour, and everyone wears white trousers, a sash and a neckerchief.

The castell tune, played on gralles (shawms) and drum, goes along with the castell while it is built. In the activity a real one plays, recorded at a castell day in Salt, and each press plays the next part.
The harp
The harp is a string instrument played by plucking the strings with the fingers.
The concert harp has 47 strings and seven pedals that change its notes.
The strings
The string family has the violins, the violas, the cellos and the double basses.
The strings are bowed or plucked with the fingers, and they are the largest group in the orchestra.
The bigger the instrument, the lower it sounds.
The woodwind
The woodwind family has the flute, the oboe, the clarinet and the bassoon.
The sound is made by blowing: in the flute the air hits an edge, and in the oboe and the clarinet it makes a reed vibrate.
Today's flute is made of metal, but it still belongs to the woodwind family.
The brass
The brass family has the trumpet, the horn, the trombone and the tuba.
The sound starts at the musician's lips, which vibrate against the mouthpiece.
The tuba is the biggest and the lowest-sounding.
The percussion
Percussion instruments are the ones that sound when they are struck, like the timpani, the triangle or the cymbals.
The orchestra's timpani are tuned, and each one plays a note.
The marimba
The marimba is a percussion instrument with wooden bars played with mallets.
Under each bar there is a tube that makes the sound resonate.
It comes from similar African instruments and is very traditional in Central America.
The harp has many tight strings that are plucked with the fingers.
The long strings play the low notes, and the short ones the high notes.
It is one of the oldest instruments known.
The marimba's wooden bars are played with soft-headed mallets.
The longer the tubes underneath, the lower the note sounds.
It has a warm, round sound that fades away slowly.
The timpani
The orchestral timpani is a large copper bowl covered with a tight skin.
A pedal tightens or loosens the skin, and that changes the note.
It is played with felt-headed sticks.
The flute
The transverse flute is held sideways and played by blowing across a hole.
The air breaking on the edge of the hole makes the sound, like when you blow across a bottle.
By covering the holes with the keys, the musician changes the notes.
The violins
The violin is the smallest and highest-sounding instrument of the string family.
It has four strings, which sound when bowed with a bow of horsehair.
There are many in the orchestra, divided into first and second violins.
The glockenspiel
The glockenspiel has metal bars that are played with hard beaters.
It sounds very high and bright, like little bells.
Its name means «set of bells» in German.
The trumpet
The trumpet is the highest instrument of the brass family.
With three valves it changes the path of the air and, in that way, the note.
The triangle
The triangle is a steel bar bent into the shape of a triangle.
It hangs from a string so that it vibrates freely and is played with a metal rod.
It makes a very high sound that lasts quite a while.
The stream
The water of a stream sounds when it hits the stones and makes little jumps.
The more stones and slope there are, the louder and livelier the sound.
The beach
The sound of the waves begins when the wave breaks and the water drags across the sand.
The waves are raised by the wind, sometimes very far from the coast.
Rain in the forest
Rain sounds when the drops hit the leaves, the ground and the puddles.
In the forest, the treetops make the rain sound soft and steady.
The crickets in the meadow
Crickets sing at night by rubbing one wing against the other.
Only the males sing, to attract the females.
The warmer it is, the faster they sing.
The frogs in the pond
Male frogs sing to attract females, above all in spring.
Many puff up a sac of skin in their throat that makes the song louder.
The blackbird in the garden
The blackbird is a black bird with a yellow beak, very common in gardens.
The male sings from a high place, above all in spring, at dawn and at dusk.
The wind on the summit
Wind is air that moves from where there is more pressure to where there is less.
On mountain tops it blows harder, and it whistles as it passes between rocks and ridges.
The bubbles on the seabed
Under water, each bubble makes a little sound because it vibrates while it forms.
Sound travels through water more than four times faster than through air.
The drops in the cave
In caves, water seeps through the rock and falls drop by drop.
Each drop leaves a little lime and, over thousands of years, forms stalactites and stalagmites.
The echo of the cave makes each drop ring out.
The narwhals
The narwhal is a toothed whale of the Arctic; the male has a long spiral tusk.
In winter it lives under the ice and breathes through the cracks that open in it.
It always lives in the cold waters of the Arctic.
The belugas
The beluga is a white whale of the Arctic; the calves are born grey and turn white over the years.
In summer it goes into estuaries and rubs itself against the pebbles on the bottom.
It makes so many whistles and songs that it is called the canary of the sea.
The bowhead whale
The bowhead whale lives all year round in the Arctic, among the ice.
With its head it can break thin ice to open a hole and breathe.
It is one of the longest-living animals: it can live for more than a hundred years.
The basking shark
The basking shark is the second largest fish in the world, after the whale shark.
It swims slowly with its mouth wide open and filters the plankton from the water.
It is harmless to people.
The humpbacks and the bubble net
Humpbacks let out air under water and make a circle of bubbles that traps the krill and the small fish.
Then they rise through the middle with their mouths open and swallow the water with the food.
The throat swells like a balloon and the water goes out again through the baleen.
The bluefin tuna
The bluefin tuna can be three metres long and swims very fast.
It crosses the Atlantic and passes through the Strait of Gibraltar to spawn in the Mediterranean.
It swims in schools that all turn at the same time.
The sperm whales
The sperm whale is the largest toothed whale and has an enormous head.
It sleeps in short naps, still and upright near the surface.
It makes very loud clicks to find its way and to communicate.
The fin whale
The fin whale is the second largest animal in the world, after the blue whale.
It is long and slender, and swims fast.
It also lives in the Mediterranean, above all in the Ligurian Sea.
The ocean sunfish
The ocean sunfish is one of the heaviest bony fish in the world.
It goes down to cold deep water to feed and then comes up to warm itself near the surface.
It eats mostly jellyfish and other soft animals.
The dolphins and the sailing boat
The striped dolphin is one of the most common dolphins in the Mediterranean.
Dolphins like to swim in the bow wave of boats: that way they move along almost without effort.
They often leap out of the water in groups.
The humpback’s leap
The humpback has the longest pectoral fins of all whales.
It leaps out of the water and falls on its back with a big splash.
In winter it goes to the warm waters of the Caribbean, where the males sing long songs.
The hammerhead sharks
The hammerhead shark has a flat, wide head, with an eye at each end.
By day it gathers in big groups around underwater mountains, and at night they split up.
It lives in warm seas all over the world.
The oarfish
The oarfish is the longest bony fish known.
It lives hundreds of metres deep, where little light reaches.
It has a red dorsal fin along its whole body.
The spinner dolphins
The spinner dolphin leaps out of the water and spins round several times in a row.
By day it rests in calm bays and at night it goes out to the open sea to feed.
It lives in groups in warm seas, such as those of Hawaii.
The whale shark
The whale shark is the largest fish in the world.
It swims with its mouth open and filters very small animals, plankton, from the water.
Each whale shark has different spots, like a fingerprint.
The manta rays
The reef manta can measure more than three metres from one wing tip to the other.
It goes to cleaning stations, where small fish remove its parasites.
It eats plankton and sometimes turns somersaults while it eats.
The dugong
The dugong is a marine mammal that eats only plants, above all seagrass.
It pulls up the grass from the bottom with its snout and leaves a furrow in the meadow.
It comes up to the surface to breathe every few minutes.
The right whale and her calf
The southern right whale has no dorsal fin and has pale callosities on its head.
Each whale has different callosities, so they can be recognised.
In winter it goes to the Valdés Peninsula, in Argentina, to have its calves.
The orcas
The orca is the largest dolphin.
It lives in very close family groups.
The male has a tall, straight dorsal fin that can be almost two metres high.
The blue whale
The blue whale is the largest animal that has ever existed.
It opens its mouth, swallows a huge amount of water with krill and its throat swells like a balloon.
Then it pushes the water out through the baleen and swallows the krill.
The valley
A river runs down a valley between mountains, passes under a stone bridge and skirts a village with a bell tower, an oak wood and some fields with a scarecrow.

The sky sings with the flute; the mountains, with the horn; the river and the village, with the harp; the forest, with the marimba, and the fields, with the udu. You hear the bell, the pigeons, a cat, a woodpecker and a hen.
When everything is painted, in spring the rainbow comes out; in summer, butterflies fly at dusk; in autumn, the leaves fall; in winter, it snows and the windows light up.
The coast
A lighthouse on top of the cliff, the sea with sailing boats, a white village perched on the hill, some stone pines on the dune and the beach with a sunshade.
The seagulls cry, a seal barks, a fish jumps and the little bell of the chapel rings. While the sea is painted, you hear the waves; in summer, the cicadas in the pines.
In winter the wind blows across the beach and the village lights up under the snow.
The high mountains
Jagged snowy peaks, a torrent running down between the meadows, a fir forest and a hamlet with a chapel.
The marmots whistle, a fish jumps in the pool, a bear growls, a woodpecker taps, a cow moos and the cowbells jingle. The torrent sounds while it is painted.
In winter the wind blows between the peaks and the windows of the hamlet light up when it snows.
The city by the sea

Hills with houses and a funicular, the harbour with cranes and a ship, a grid of rooftops with a church, a park with plane trees and a merry-go-round, and the promenade with palm trees and a Ferris wheel.
You hear the ship’s horn, the tram bell, the pigeons in the park, a cat on the rooftops and the seagulls in the harbour.
When the rooftops are painted, the tram goes by and stops at the stop; in winter, the city lights up under the snow.
The lake and the volcanoes
Two sleeping volcanoes behind a still lake with a boat, a beech wood, some farmhouses and fields with two windmills.
A raven croaks, the fish jump, a duck quacks, a wild boar snorts, a hen clucks and the windmill sails turn. The windmills sound while the fields are painted.
In summer a balloon takes off and a kite flies; in autumn, the leaves of the beech wood fly all over the landscape.
Grandma Pepa and the omelette on the ceiling
Grandma flips the omelette so high that it sticks to a beam. She waits underneath, stamps her feet, and has an idea: a plate on her head.
The omelette comes unstuck and falls onto the plate. In the second round it lands on the head of the cat, who was asleep on top of the stove.
Her voice is the clarinet.
Grandpa Tomàs goes fishing
Grandpa is asleep with his rod. The float sinks, a tug wakes him up and the carp flies out of the pond onto his hat.
Its tail tickles his nose; he tries to grab it and the carp jumps back into the water. In the second round, an old boot comes out first.
His voice is the horn.
Nina and the giant carrot
Nina pulls a leaf with all her strength: out comes a tiny carrot and she falls on her bottom.
She pulls the next one, the ground swells and a giant carrot lifts her into the air. She climbs up, waves and slides down.
Her voice is the flute.
Pol and the wind at the washing line
Pol hangs up the washing on tiptoe. A gust takes his cap and a stronger one lifts the sheet with him hanging on.
He flies over the yard and lands in the haystack with his legs in the air; he comes out with straw on his head and his cap on backwards.
The sheet covers Grandpa, who snores like a ghost. His voice is the glockenspiel.
Nata the goat and the shower of figs
Nata wants figs. She stands up, can’t reach, backs off, scrapes the ground and charges the trunk: boom!
It rains figs: one gets stuck between her horns and one falls into her mouth. A sunny shower, a shake and out comes the rainbow.
She ends up on the swing. Her voice is the marimba.
Supper outdoors
At dusk, the family has supper under the fig tree with lanterns. Grandma brings the omelette; Grandpa’s carp jumps into the jug.
They make a toast, they eat, and Nata pulls the tablecloth. Night falls: stars, fireflies and the lit windows.
The family theme plays: the flute and the clarinet with the whole band.
The hot-air balloon
The burner heats the air inside the fabric. Hot air weighs less than the cold air around it, and that is why the balloon rises.
When the burner goes off, the air slowly cools and the balloon comes down.
A balloon cannot be steered: the wind pushes it, and up high it usually blows harder than near the ground.
Fields, farmhouses, flocks of sheep and villages with bell towers.
The train crosses the river on a stone viaduct with arches.
At the end of the valley, a reservoir holds the river’s water.
A fishing harbour, beaches and coves with pine trees.
The white villages look out to sea and the seagulls fly over the islets.
On the cape there is a lighthouse: at night, its light turns to warn the ships.
A mountain hut among pines, cold-water lakes and scree slopes.
The chamois leap across the rocks and the ravens fly over the cliffs.
The cable car carries people up, hanging from a steel cable.
The delta
Where the river reaches the sea there are rice fields, canals and white cottages with reed roofs.
Ducks and flamingos live in the lagoons.
The sand dunes end at the river mouth, where the river water meets the sea water.
The islands
Windmills, coves of clear water and villages perched on the hill.
An old castle watches over the sea from above.
Dolphins leap near the coast and a small lighthouse marks the island at night.
A whole day and the seasons
Each journey lasts a day: from dawn to midday, sunset, night and the small hours.
In spring there is a shower and the rainbow comes out; in summer, a distant storm; in autumn, fog and geese; in winter, snow.
When day breaks again, the balloon lands where people are waiting for it with lanterns.

The skittles
A player of Catalan skittles throws the throwing stick at six skittles in two rows of three.

Surprises: the domino effect, the skittle that dances and stays standing, the streetlamp that sends the stick back, the dog that fetches it, the candyfloss and the skittles that go back to their places by themselves.
Finale: the six skittles dance in a ring and the player takes a bow. Music: a polka with clarinet, tuba and pizzicato violins.
The human cannonball
An acrobat shoots out of the cannon with a cotton-wool «boom».
Surprises: the net, the band’s kettledrum, the straw cannonball, the trampoline that sends him back into the cannon, the elephant that catches him with its trunk and the umbrella to float down.
Finale: he lands upright on a little chair on top of a pole and takes a bow. Music: a paso doble with trumpet, tuba and snare drum.
The wind-up rocket
A boy winds up the tin rocket and steps back.
Surprises: the parachute, the loop round the moon, the stuck star, the curl of smoke, the corkscrews and the cardboard box it jumps out of.
Finale: the moon opens like a tin box and a shower of stars falls out. Music: a waltz with flute, cellos and pizzicato violins.
The strength tester
A strongman with a moustache hits the lever with a wooden mallet and the puck shoots up the tower.
Surprises: the puck that stops halfway up, the bell, the tower that stretches like an accordion, the nest, the swinging bell and the strongman who goes flying.
Finale: the bulbs on the tower light up and the bell plays a tune. Music: a march with horn, tuba and bass drum.
The horse race

Surprises: a win by a nose, the horse that stops to eat a flower, the dead heat, the jump, the backwards lap and the run-down horse pushed by the other one.
Finale: the rails curve and the horses become a turning merry-go-round. Music: a galop with clarinet, tuba and claves.
Poppy
It grows in cereal fields and along the edges of paths, in spring.
The bud hangs upside down and straightens up before opening; the two hairy sepals fall off when the flower opens.
It has four red petals, crumpled like tissue paper, with a dark blotch at the base. A bee visits it.
Daisy
What looks like a single flower is a flower head: a head with many little florets together.
The white florets round the edge look like petals; the yellow ones in the middle are tiny tube-shaped florets.
It grows in meadows in spring and summer. A white butterfly arrives.
Sunflower
Its head is also a flower head, with hundreds of florets.
The florets in the middle form crossing spirals, some going one way and some the other.
When young, the head follows the sun during the day; when grown, it stays facing east. A bumblebee arrives.
Cornflower
Each «petal» is a funnel-shaped floret with a toothed edge.
It used to grow in every wheat field; now it is harder to find.
A ladybird walks along the edge of the flower.
White water lily
It lives in ponds: its round leaves float on the water.
The flower opens in the morning, petal by petal, and closes in the afternoon.
A dragonfly flies low over the water.
Lotus
The leaves and flowers rise above the water.
In the middle it has a flat receptacle with holes, where the seeds form.
Water slides off its leaves and leaves them clean. A frog jumps onto the leaf.
Yellow iris
It grows on the banks of rivers and ponds.
It has three big drooping parts, with dark stripes that guide insects to the nectar.
Its leaves are long like swords. A red dragonfly stops on it.
Calla lily
What looks like a white petal is a spathe: a leaf that wraps around the yellow spadix.
The real flowers are tiny and sit on the spadix.
It lives in damp places and comes from southern Africa. Drops of water slide off it.
Foxglove
The thimble-shaped flowers open from the bottom of the stem to the top.
The spots inside guide the bumblebees, which go all the way in to look for nectar.
It is very poisonous: look, but do not touch.
Cyclamen
The flower hangs upside down and the petals turn upwards, like flames.
The leaves are heart-shaped, with silvery markings.
It grows in the shade of woods. A snail goes slowly by.
Violet
It smells sweet and flowers at the end of winter and in spring.
It has five petals; the bottom one has lines that guide insects.
It grows in the shade, at the foot of trees. A brown butterfly arrives.
Peony
The peony grows in woods and in mountain meadows.
The big, crumpled petals open into a bowl, around a crown of yellow stamens.
It flowers at the end of spring. A blackbird looks for worms on the ground.
Moonflower
It opens in the evening and closes in the morning.
It unfolds in a few minutes, twisting open like a paper umbrella.
At night, its white can be seen from far away. A moth visits it.
Madonna lily
It has six white tepals and long stamens with golden pollen.
As it opens, the edges of the tepals grow more than the middle: that is why they ripple and curl back.
It smells strongly in the evening. The fireflies light up to find each other.
Camellia
It flowers in winter and at the beginning of spring.
In this form, the petals are arranged in a perfect spiral and open from the outside in.
It comes from East Asia; the tea plant belongs to the same family.
Jasmine
It makes clusters of small, white, star-shaped flowers with five petals.
The buds are pink and open one after another.
It has a very strong scent, above all in the evening and at night.
Orchid
It has three sepals, two petals as wide as wings and a third petal, the lip, which is a landing strip for insects.
It comes from the rainforests of Asia; at home it lives in a greenhouse or near a window.
A blue butterfly arrives.
Hibiscus
It has five big petals that open in a spiral.
From the middle comes a long column with the pollen and five red stigmas at the tip.
Each flower lasts only one day. A hummingbird drinks its nectar.
Passion flower
It has ten white parts and a crown of blue, white and purple filaments.
In the middle there are five anthers and three stigmas.
Carpenter bees, big and black, carry its pollen.
Bird of paradise
The flower comes out of a green beak, like a bird’s head.
The orange sepals and the blue arrow-shaped petals open one after another.
When a bird perches on it, the pollen sticks to its feet.
Turkish
Big and small stones with fine veins of another colour between them: the oldest European pattern.
First a few big drops and many small ones fall; those of the second colour fall between the stones and keep them apart with veins.
Bookbinding workshop in Barcelona: guitar, clarinet, double bass and tambourine, in three time.
Spanish
Two-colour stones crossed by fine diagonal waves.
After the drops, a diagonal puff of wind makes the water slide in fine waves.
Papers like this were used to cover the boards and endpapers of books.
Combed
Vertical stripes that the stylus pulls back and forth and a fine comb combs.
Each note leaves a line of ink that widens into a stripe; the stylus pulls them back and forth and each tooth of the comb leaves a line of every colour.
The guitar plays when the drops fall; the harp, when the comb passes.
Peacock
A combed two-colour chequerboard that ends in peacock feathers.
The drops fall in a two-colour chequerboard; then, three passes: the stylus, a fine comb and a comb that makes waves.
At the end, the paper is laid on the water and takes up the print.
Bordered stones
Three-colour stones with a dark edge and a free S-shaped stroke of the stylus.
The dark edge is pigment that gathers at the rim of each drop; then the stylus crosses the bath in an S.
Ebru workshop in Istanbul: harp, oboe, udu and drum, in 9/8 time.
There and back
Diagonal rows of drops that the stylus crosses up and down.
The drops fall in slanting rows of two colours; the stylus, up and down, turns them into flames.
Ebru has been on UNESCO’s list of Intangible Cultural Heritage since 2014.
Chain of hearts
A row of coloured bullseyes: a single stroke of the stylus turns them into hearts.
The drops fall in turn on four centres and make bullseyes; the stylus passes once through the middle of them all and each bullseye becomes a heart.
The harp glides as the stylus passes; the udu plays the bass.
Tulip
A frame of stones all round and a big tulip drawn in the middle.
Some big drops in the middle and coloured stones all round, closing in like a frame; then the stylus pulls out the tulip’s petals.
The oboe sings the melody and the drum keeps the beat.
Rings
Rings of ink and water around a few centres, moved by a fan.
In suminagashi, ink and clear water touch the bath in turn and make rings.
Suminagashi workshop in Kyoto: harp, marimba and claves.
Fan
Three centres of two-colour rings that a puff of wind ripples like cloth.
In suminagashi there is no comb: the rings are moved by blowing or with a fan.
The harp plays at each drop; the claves keep the beat.
Ripple
Diagonal centres and the stylus passing slowly, making waves.
Four diagonal centres; a single slow pass of the stylus stretches the rings without breaking them.
The marimba plays the melody over the harp.
Wheel
A single big centre with rings of three colours, and the stylus circling it, each time the other way.
All the drops fall on the same centre, ink and water in turn; the stylus circles it, each time the other way, and the rings zigzag.
In Japan, papers like this survive from the 12th century.
French curl
Overlapping rows of three-colour drops, a fine comb and, on top, little curls in a row.
The drops fall in overlapping rows; each curl is the stylus making a small turn, now one way, now the other.
Paris workshop: piano, pizzicato violins and cellos, glockenspiel and triangle.
Bouquet
Wavy rows of drops, fine combing and a wide comb that makes bouquets.
The drops fall in rows that make waves; then, three passes: the stylus, the fine comb and a wide comb that makes waves.
When the comb passes, the piano plays a scale.
Star
A huge coloured bullseye and the stylus drawing rays from the centre outwards and from the outside to the centre.
All the drops fall in the centre and make a huge bullseye; the stylus crosses it in twelve rays and then goes back from the outside in.
The pizzicato cellos play the bass and the triangle keeps the beat.
Rose
A crown of drops round the centre and a big rose drawn with the stylus.
One big drop in the middle and three rings of drops round it, each a different colour; the stylus draws the petals.
Then the paper dries on the line with the other sheets.
Old Dutch
Rows of drops in alternating colours, the stylus going back and forth, one comb and another across.
The drops fall in rows of alternating colours, ordered like the letters on a page; at the end, a comb across.
The printer’s workshop in Nuremberg: marimba, bassoon, flute, glockenspiel and claves.
Zigzag
Four-colour stripes that the stylus, from side to side, turns into zigzags.
Each note leaves a line of ink that widens into a stripe; when the stylus goes from side to side in a zigzag, all the stripes follow it.
When the stylus passes, the marimba plays a scale.
Spiral
Drops spiralling from the centre and the stylus circling them until everything turns.
The drops fall along a spiral; in the centre the ink turns more than at the edge, and that is why a spiral appears.
The flute sings the melody and the bassoon plays the bass.
Whirlpool
Two coloured bullseyes and three whirlpools that carry them off.
Two three-colour bullseyes; the whirlpools at the sides turn one way and the one in the middle the other way.
Each drop and each gesture moves the ink, but none is made or lost.
Soap bubbles
A bubble is a film of soapy water much thinner than a hair. The light reflected from its two faces interferes, and each thickness of the film makes a different colour shine.
Without weight, the bubbles float and wobble when they touch. Two bubbles stuck together share a wall, and where three films meet they always make angles of 120 degrees.
When a bubble bursts, the hole opens from one point at a constant speed. Here it is shown much more slowly than in reality.
Plasma

A gas does not conduct electricity until the electric field is strong enough to tear electrons off the atoms. Then channels of ionised gas open up and give off light, as in a plasma ball or a lightning bolt.
The channels grow mostly where the field is strongest and they branch. When a channel reaches another electrode, the arc jumps across; it carries all the current and is what shines brightest.
The computer works out the electric field at every moment. A real discharge crosses the gap in millionths of a second: here it goes a million times slower so that its shape can be seen.
Water spheres
Without gravity, as on the space station, water does not fall: surface tension pulls it until it makes a ball, the shape with the least surface.
Two balls that touch join into one and wobble for a while, more slowly the bigger they are. Each spout squirts water of one colour, and the colours mix inside the balls that join.
The computer solves the equations of the water and the air. The water in the simulation is thicker than real water so that the calculation stays stable.
Smoke rings

When a puff of air comes out of a slit, the edges make it roll over itself and a vortex ring forms that moves forward on its own and carries the smoke. You see a cross-section of the ring: two eddies turning opposite ways.
Two rings that collide head-on spread out sideways, and a ring that catches up with another from behind passes through it. The smoke only makes the movement of the air visible.
The computer works out the movement of the air. The air in the simulation is thicker than real air, and that is why the rings are wider and stop sooner.
Lava lamp
Cold wax weighs a little more than the liquid in the lamp and rests at the bottom. The bulb heats it: warm wax expands, becomes lighter than the liquid and rises.
At the top it cools, gets heavier again and sinks. The shapes of the drops, the necks that narrow and the drops that join come from the equations: they are not drawn.
It is the only matter in the activity that has weight. Here everything goes faster than in a real lamp, which takes quite a while to warm up.
Ferrofluid
A ferrofluid is a liquid full of tiny magnetic particles. Without a magnetic field it is a smooth black puddle, like a mirror.

Each press sends more current through the coil. When the field passes a certain value, the flat surface can no longer hold and rises into a row of spikes; the stronger the field, the taller and sharper they are.
The distance between the spikes comes from the balance between magnetic force, surface tension and weight. The computer works out the field and the liquid at every moment.
Oil and water
Water and oil do not mix. Here they are between two glass plates very close together, lit from behind, and each press pushes in water with ink.
When a thin liquid pushes a thicker one, the edge does not move forward flat: any bump goes faster than those beside it and becomes a finger, which splits and branches.
This is viscous fingering, the same thing that happens when water is injected underground to get oil out.
Nebula
A nebula is a dark cloud of hydrogen where stars are born. The ultraviolet light of a new, very massive star tears electrons off the surrounding gas, and that gas glows.
The glowing gas, much hotter, pushes the cloud and opens a growing bubble. Behind the knots of dense gas a shadow remains: a pillar pointing at the star, like those in the Eagle Nebula.
In the end the stars explode as supernovae and the shock waves sweep the gas away. In the computer, what takes millions of years in space happens in seconds.
The twenty forms of nature, in the order of the activity, and why each one repeats itself within itself.
Ferns
Each fern frond is made of pinnae with the same shape as the frond, and each pinna of smaller pieces with the same shape. This repetition of a shape at different scales is what we call a fractal.
Young fronds are born rolled up in a spiral, like the head of a bishop’s crook, and unroll as they grow.
Four simple rules (shrink, turn and shift), repeated thousands of times, are enough for a computer to draw a fern that looks real.
Snowflakes

A snowflake has six arms because the water molecules of ice link up in hexagons. The tips stick out into the damp air, receive more vapour and grow faster: so branches come out, and from them, smaller branches.

The six arms look so alike because they grow at the same time and go through the same temperature and humidity as the flake falls. The most branched stars form at about fifteen degrees below zero, in very damp air.
Mathematicians imagined an ideal flake, Koch’s, in which every side is divided without end: its edge is infinitely long and yet it encloses a limited area.

What looks like one flower is a head of hundreds of small florets, and the «petals» around the edge are flowers too. Each floret is born turned about 137.5 degrees from the one before, the golden angle, and so they fill the disc without gaps.
With this angle, spirals appear in both directions, and if you count them you very often get two consecutive numbers of the Fibonacci sequence, such as 34 and 55 or 55 and 89.
The same way of sharing out the pieces is found in pine cones, in the scales of pineapples and in the leaves of many plants around the stem.
Lightning
Lightning does not come down all at once: a channel of charged air moves towards the ground in jumps of a few tens of metres, and at each jump it can split into branches that split again.

When one of the branches touches the ground, the current runs through it with all its force and that path shines much brighter than the others. The branches that did not reach the ground remain as a finer tracery.
The same branchings appear when a discharge goes through a block of plastic or wood. They have a fractal dimension of about 1.7: more than a line (1) and less than a surface (2).
Tree
Each branch of a tree looks like a smaller tree, and each twig like a branch: the same rule of splitting is repeated up to the tips, where the leaves and flowers come out.
Leonardo da Vinci already noticed that when a branch splits, the daughter branches together are about as thick as the mother: the total cross-section is kept from level to level.
With this shape the tree puts many leaves in the sun and, at the same time, carries water from the roots to the last leaf along short paths.
River and tributaries

A river gathers the water of a whole territory through a network of tributaries: brooks that join into streams and streams that join into rivers. Seen from the air, each piece of the network looks like the whole network.

Geographers number the stretches: two first-order brooks make one of the second order, two of the second, one of the third, up to the main river. All over the world, each order has three to five times fewer stretches than the one before.
The network spreads until hardly any corner is left far from a brook: it is a line that tends to fill a surface.
A branching coral is a colony of thousands of small polyps, relatives of sea anemones. Each polyp builds a limestone skeleton beneath it, and when new ones are born the branch grows longer or splits.
The branches share out the space to catch the light and the water that brings food, and the same way of splitting is repeated from the thick branches to the tips.
Inside the polyps live microscopic algae that give them food and colour. When the water gets too warm, the polyps expel them and the coral turns white.
Each cone of the Romanesco is made of smaller cones set in a spiral, and each of these is made again of even smaller cones. Several levels can be followed with the naked eye.
The spirals follow the same golden angle as the sunflower, and if you count them in each direction you get numbers of the Fibonacci sequence.
It happens because the buds that should make flowers never quite do: each one turns into a stem that makes buds again, which do not flower either, and the process repeats faster and faster.
Neurons
Neurons receive signals from other neurons through their dendrites, extensions that branch like a tree: from the body of the cell come branches that split again and again.
By branching like this, a single neuron can reach thousands of other neurons with very little wiring. Some large neurons of the cerebellum receive more than a hundred thousand contacts.
With experience and learning, dendrites gain or lose small branches and spines: the shape of the tree changes throughout life.
Island and coast
The lines of this island are contour lines, like those on maps: each one joins the points at the same height, from the summit down to the coastline.

How long is a coast? It depends on the ruler: the shorter it is, the more inlets and headlands it picks up and the longer the measurement comes out. It is the example the mathematician Benoît Mandelbrot used to explain fractals.

Bays have smaller bays, and these have coves and rocks: at every scale the coast is just as irregular. That is why in a photo it is hard to guess whether you see a hundred metres or a hundred kilometres.

The veins carry water to the whole leaf and take away the sugar that light makes in it. From the midrib come the secondary veins, from these the tertiary ones, down to a network so fine that no cell is far from a vein.
Unlike a tree, the fine network closes into loops: if an insect cuts a vein, the water can go round and still arrive.
Very old plants, like the ginkgo, have veins that only fork, without loops.
Frost on the window
When the glass of a window is much colder than the damp air inside, water vapour sticks to it directly as ice, without first turning into liquid water.

The ice starts at a scratch or a speck of dust and grows in needles. The tips stick out, receive more vapour and grow faster; new ones are born from them, and so feathers that look like ferns are formed.
It is the same thing that makes the branches of snowflakes grow, but on a flat surface.
Nautilus

The nautilus is a relative of the octopus that lives inside a shell. As it grows it builds new chambers, each a little larger than the one before, and closes off the old ones with a wall; the gas inside helps it float.
Since the chambers always grow in the same proportion, the shell has the same shape whether small or large: it is a logarithmic spiral, and a piece of the shell is a small copy of the whole.
It is often said to follow the golden ratio, but measurements show it does not: each shell has its own proportion, and it is almost never that one.
Mycelium
The mushroom is only the fruit: the fungus lives underground as a network of very fine threads, the hyphae, which grow at their tips and branch. All together they form the mycelium.
When a tip finds food, the network strengthens that path and makes it thicker; where it finds none, the branches stop. So it explores the soil with as little thread as possible.
Many fungi join the roots of trees and give them water and minerals in exchange for sugars. Under a forest in Oregon, a single fungus covers almost ten square kilometres.
Cracked mud
When mud dries, the top layer shrinks but the bottom holds it back, and the tension cracks it. First some long cracks open and divide the ground into large pieces.
Then each piece cracks inside, and the new cracks end on the old ones at right angles: pieces within pieces, smaller and smaller.
If the mud is wetted and dried many times, the right-angled joints slowly turn until they make angles of 120 degrees, like the basalt columns that form when lava cools.
Peacock feather

A feather is a tree with three levels: from the shaft come the barbs, and from each barb, hundreds of barbules. In flight feathers, the barbules hook together with tiny hooks and make a closed surface.

The peacock’s colours are not pigments: inside the barbules there are neatly ordered rods of melanin that reflect only certain colours of light, like a soap bubble. That is why the colour changes when the feather moves.
The «eyes» of the train are for courtship: the male raises the feathers in a fan and makes them quiver in front of the female.
Mountain ranges
A mountain range has a main ridge from which spurs come out, and from the spurs, smaller spurs. Between each pair a stream carves a valley: ridges and valleys are two networks fitted into each other.
Seen from far or near, a mountain is just as rugged: a rock can look like a peak. That is why geology photos put an object beside it, so that its size can be seen.
The mountains of many films are made by computer by repeating a rule: divide the ground, raise or sink each piece a little at random, and divide again.
Roots
From a main root come lateral roots, and from these, even finer roots covered in root hairs. Branching lets the plant explore a lot of soil to find water and minerals.
Roots grow at the tip and sense where there is more water or more food: there they branch more, and where the soil is poor they grow little.
A classic study measured all the roots of a single four-month-old rye plant: they added up to about 600 kilometres, and counting the root hairs, more than 10,000.
Shell of triangles
Some cone shells have a pattern of triangles of every size, very like the Sierpinski triangle, a fractal made of triangles within triangles.

The pattern is painted at the edge of the shell as it grows, line by line. Each cell of the edge lays down pigment or not depending on what its neighbours do: some pass the activity on and others switch it off.
Very simple programs, cellular automata, do the same: with a few rules between neighbours they create patterns of great complexity.
The white ball is the fruit of a whole head of florets: each floret leaves a seed with a long beak and, on top, a pappus of about a hundred filaments spread like the ribs of an umbrella.
Air flows between the filaments and, just above the pappus, a ring-shaped vortex forms that does not come away and brakes it. So the seed falls very slowly, and with wind it can travel kilometres.
The shape repeats at every scale: the head carries seeds, each seed carries a pappus, and each filament has small teeth along its sides.
